newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentina restores ancestral lands to Colla Indians.
newsitem.headline: Argentina restores ancestral lands to Colla Indians.

text.p: Argentina finally restored to the Colla Indians of its northwest region the ownership of their ancestral lands on Wednesday, half a century after they first marched on Buenos Aires to demand their rights.

About 100 Collas, whose lands in the mountain provinces of Salta and Jujuy were once the southernmost outpost of the Inca empire, travelled to the capital to receive deeds personally to 308,900 acres (125,000 hectares) from President Carlos Menem.
In 1946 their parents had come on foot and mule and got little more than promises from the president at that time, Gen. Juan Peron.

This time they came by bus. Dressed in broad-rimmed hats and red ponchos that looked oddly out of place among the gilt and and colonial uniforms of Government House, they sang and beat drums to celebrate the first expropriation of private land for native Indian peoples.

"It is the recognition of the right to land occupied by people who were always its real owners, after a long struggle that has not lasted 10, 20 or 30 years, but centuries," said the Peronist president in a speech.

With state land that has already been given up under laws included in 1994's constitutional reforms, Menem has now returned 3.954 million acres (1.6 million hectares) to some of Argentina's 600,000 indigenous people and plans to hand over 988,400 acres (400,000 hectares) more by 1999.
"Rest assured that we will not stop until all our Indian brothers are the owners once again of lands that were unjustly usurped," said Menem.

Like many of the 200,000 Collas living in the northwest, the peasant farmers from the Finca Santiago who had their land restored to them have been living there for generations, paying rent since colonial times to farm their own ancestral land.
"Until now the land wasn't ours and the owners were always threatening to evict us, so we didn't improve the land," said 60-year-old Sergio Canchi.
"The rent was very expensive and we can't get jobs to pay it because we can't read. But now we are going to grow beans and potatos and maize," said his neighbour, Miguel Angel, 57.

Colla lawyer Eulogio Frites, seeing a lifetime campaign bear fruit, told Reuters the Collas would fight on "so that all of Argentina's Indians get back their land, their forests and their natural resources."

Social Development Secretary Eduardo Amadeus criticised a recent resolution made by the European Parliament urging Argentina to start defending indigenous people's rights, especially the Mapuche Indians of Patagonia.

"The indigenous people have been abandoned to the mercy of God," he told Reuters. "But now we are taking action and these European Parliament people who come here knowing nothing about it make me angry. They should recognise what we are doing."
Menem rejected any link between his new drive on Indian rights and upcoming elections in Congress: "These are strictly acts of justice and nothing to do with politics."
